title: E10: Investing Early and Making Your Own Luck with Mac Conwell - Investing in Startups | Podcast on Spotify

text:
[SPEAKER_00]
What's up? Welcome back to Seed to Harvest, a podcast focusing on stories and tactics from a diverse array of investors, founders, and creators, hosted by me, Paige Van Doherty. I'm the founding partner behind Genius Ventures and the author of an illustrated children's book about venture, also called Seed to Harvest.

[SPEAKER_01]
You can do venture differently. You don't have to follow anybody's path. When you want to do something that people think is crazy, you'll get a lot of naysayers. Just do it.

[SPEAKER_00]
I'm really excited to be here today with Matt Conwell, the founding partner of Rare Breed Ventures and an enthusiastic drag racer. Before we hop into today's episode, a quick word from our sponsor. If you're a startup founder, you know early decisions can be the difference between success and failure. One decision that thousands of successful founders have made is choosing Stripe as their payments platform. Fun fact, at Seed to Harvest, I used Stripe Atlas to incorporate my company. It was super easy and simple to incorporate my company, especially with their thorough instructions. I was able to set up a bank account and start accepting payments through Stripe. And over the past decade, Stripe has supported the growth of the most ambitious businesses, including Shopify, Lyft, and Kickstarter. Stripe uniquely knows how to support startups from their Atlas product that allows you to turn your idea into a business by helping you incorporate quickly, to their capital product that provides funding to help you scale your startup. Stripe has the tools you need to grow your business. And if you want to learn how Stripe can support you, visit Stripe.com today. That's Stripe.com to get started today. Now let's dive in. I'm really excited to share a bit of Mac's story, how he spends his time and how he makes investment decisions. So what is your North Star, Mac?

[SPEAKER_01]
So my North Star is this amazing black woman here in Baltimore. I watched this woman for three years try to convince people that her idea of a tumble dryer that can dry a wig or hair extension in 15 minutes with no heat was a valuable idea. I watched her get nothing but no's to the point where she determined that her only option in order to get access to capital to start building her first prototype was by becoming a surrogate mother. She gave birth to twins to raise a nominal amount of money just so she could start building a prototype. And to watch her go through that experience was truly frustrating for me, especially considering when you look at the wig and hair extension market, which is predicted to be a $10 billion market by the year 2023, with zero innovation in the care for the products, what she was building was like a true opportunity. And nobody else could see that.

[SPEAKER_00]
I think that's such an incredibly powerful story of what motivates you as an investor. So I believe that congratulations are in order as you have closed your first fund.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yes, we have closed fund one, a rare breed.

[SPEAKER_00]
All the flowers. I'm so happy for you, Mac. It's been such an incredible year, two years to be on this journey together. So I would love to hear more about like your experience fundraising, some of the fun and not so fun stories that came out of that.

[SPEAKER_01]
Fundraising is hard. You know, everybody talks about how hard it is. And then you start doing it and you realize it is like as hard, if not harder than what everybody says. Early on in the fundraising process, I recognized I didn't have a network of LPs. But I noticed that the more I tweeted about venture and entrepreneurship, the more other VCs will follow me. And so I just made it a point that if I saw there was a VC who followed me, I would send them a message to have a meeting. And so I had a lot of meetings in a short amount of time, but it did three things. One, it helped grow my profile and brand because now I had a larger group of people who knew me. Two, it helped me learn like how to fundraise and from other GPs and get advice. But then three, and the one that I wasn't expecting but was most important was a lot of these GPs, other funds started committing capital to my fund. And so like the first two to three million in my fund, which is a $10 million fund, all came from, the majority came from other GPs, other funds. And so like the Twitter thing became my strategy. And then also on top of that, AngelList last year came out, or in 2020, came out with their rolling funds. And, you know, those things started to get popular. One of the really interesting parts about rolling funds was they were able to publicly solicit. And so my Twitter presence is growing. I'm like, oh, the ability to publicly solicit would be a game changer for me. I got to do this. And really what it was is they were taking advantage of a designation that most funds hadn't, a 506C. The 506C designation actually comes from the Jobs Act from back in 2013, which allows for both funds and companies to raise capital in a public manner, but all their investors must be accredited. So for me, that gave me a clear option to talk about my fund publicly. And now I'm part of a wave that you, I would say, are part of as well, of these emerging funds that are doing what we call building in public, where we're keeping people involved and letting people know what we're doing at every step of the way in a very transparent way. It was allowing a lot of people to see how the industry works. And so I want to ask you, Paige, what's that been like for you, building in public? How's building in public been for you?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, building in public's been super interesting. We've had a bit of divergent routes because we chose to raise under 506B, which means you can't solicit and you can't publicly talk about fundraising. So I honestly struggled with that. It was interesting walking the line of how can I add value to the community that I've built while staying compliant. But I think that I've been so excited to see you and the folks at Overlooked, especially, have just done an incredible job of bringing the community into your fundraising process and talking about how difficult it is. There was a great quote from Harry Stebbings' podcast about, he said, everyone talks about how hard fundraising is and says it's the hardest thing they've ever done. And then you actually start doing it and you're like, oh, wow, this is definitely the hardest thing that I've ever done. That's the one thing I wish I could have shared more of is it is a very difficult journey. But it's sometimes like you have to laugh at it. Like getting your first million dollar no is such a surreal, surreal experience.

[SPEAKER_01]
There's nothing positive about getting the no.

[SPEAKER_00]
It's just not yet.

[SPEAKER_01]
No, it's not. I mean, it's interesting for context. From June of 2020, September of 2020, I had over 1,100 meetings, right? And from like June 2020 to June of 2021, I had close to 4,000 meetings. So I just had a bunch of meetings, right? And so I never went into them thinking about money as I was about learning and making connections if the money happened, great. And so when people would pass, I'd be like, well, I never asked for it anyway, so thanks. It's cool. I don't have a GP commit, which, you know, other GPs can be mad at me about. I'm sorry. I just, I'm broke. Like, I mean, if you can't get over the fact that I don't have the money to be able to put in my own capital into this fund, and you think that's going to stop me from doing everything humanly possible? Like, the whole point of putting in a GP commit is just so that they can feel like you have skin in the game. So, like, they feel like you're going to be attached to this fund as they are. It's like, no, this is my career. Like, if this fund doesn't work, like, I'm out of work, essentially. You know, my track record's not as long, so I've had LPs passed for that, you know. I probably have had LPs passed because I'm big, black, and with dreadlocks. I don't know. I can only surmise, right? But I will say, you know, we all have these moments in fundraising. But as you go, you have these moments where, like, you get on the winning streak where, like, every meeting you have, you're closing and you're winning and you're feeling good. And you're like, oh, this fund's going to be closed in no time. And then all of a sudden you get a no that you weren't expecting or a string of no's. And it just kind of resets you. Like, I was used to that. But I will say, you know, I've had talks with other fund managers where, like, those moments come up and it's like, dang, I wasn't prepared for that. No. I got to reset myself and, like, take a day and get ready to get back up on the horse and go back at it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Oh, yeah. That, like, regulation of your – I refer to it as an emotional thermostat. But how you stay regulated during such an incredibly rollercoaster style of emotions. I'm curious how that has changed for you. I remember watching this video when we first started raising and someone committed to a $10,000 investment. And I took a video and I was crying in it because I was so happy.

[SPEAKER_01]
I don't know if I thought about it too much because, like, again, I should say, like, raising a fund as a fund manager is the most entrepreneurial thing we can do. Right. Mm-hmm. And having had two startups before, like, it just all looked really familiar. And then I realized, like, oh, yeah, I'm building a company from scratch again. I said I would never do this. This is awesome. And so it's just more the regulation of you enjoy the wins and you try not to beat yourself up for the losers. Right. But I will say, you know, there's been several times where I've gotten the call and people have committed and I've, like, gone run around in my backyard screaming and yelling, like, I can't believe it. We did this. You know, the first time somebody committed a dollar to my fund. The first time I got the $100,000 check. Shout out to Scott Telsky. The first time I got, you know, a $500,000 check, which turned into a million check. Shout out Insight Partners. All of those were seminal moments for me that let me know, like, oh, like, this is possible. But then, you know, when you get the nose or you get turned down or when you have a meeting, like, everything is going great and then there's some technicality that comes up later or there's some due diligence thing that you're like, yeah, I'm not doing this 20-page due diligence package. Y'all can keep your money kind of. Those things are deflating. But, you know, I've gone through that grind before. And so, you know, it's just, all right, you know, take an evening, watch a basketball game, watch a football game, have an old-fashioned, and go back to it tomorrow, right? Like, you just internalize and you've got to go. Go to Buffalo Wild Wings. Go to Buffalo Wild Wings with your friends and vent about it. And then, you know, you go back to it. So that's really, you know, everybody's got to find their own way to kind of de-stress and let that stuff go. And you just can't dwell on it.

[SPEAKER_00]
It's hard learning how to take things, like, less seriously while appreciating the privilege that you have for being in the position that you're in. I'm curious, you mentioned earlier that your fund structure is different. I would love if you could expand on that.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, so I should say my basic structure of my fund is fairly standard. It's more about the process that we put in place for fundraising. It was really abnormal. And what I recognized was all the things I liked about rolling funds were, like, technological. And all the things I hated were structural. And I was like, well, if I just use the standard structure, can I do everything else the same? The answer was pretty much yes, right? So, you know, 506C, public solicit, work with Carta as a back office. They had a partnership at the time with a company called Anduin Transactions, which turns your sub docs and LPA and any other legal docs into a guided web form, which is awesome because all I got to do is send people links and they can get access to my docs. And so you can go to rarebreed.vc and click a button to become an LP. Tell us you're accredited and you will just automatically get access to our sub docs. Like, you ain't got to talk to me. You ain't got to worry about the lawyer. Like, you just go straight there. And we do rolling closes every three weeks. So as LPs commit, we would send them to Carta and Batches. And every three weeks we would close on a group of LPs, which allowed us to get capital as we were going. We gave our LPs three options for capital. I got the idea for that from 500 Startups Fund 1, where they made all their LPs put 50% up front and 25% each year over the next two years, which is like rolling fund is like people subscribe for quarters. So we basically gave people the ability to subscribe for years. We could do 100% up front, 50% over two years, or 33% each year for three years, with the minimum being 10K per year. So if you wanted to make a 10K investment, you had to do it all up front. I haven't had a single LP yet. I have a concern about it, which also reminded me that like all the things they tell you that you're supposed to do in venture, like you don't have to follow any rules. Like there aren't really rules here, right? Like there are structures and processes that have worked in the past for others, and they've just shared it enough where that became the prevailing thought, but doesn't have to be the only one, right? And so like those are the kind of things that we did differently. But, you know, the back-end structure, you know, there's a management company, a GP, an LP, right? LPs don't want things that are too crazy, too out of the ordinary, right?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, you don't want like half your pitch to be explaining like some weird aspect of your back-end.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yes, like that's not helpful. But also that's one of the reasons why I did some of those long-form posts that I did. So like I did a post about we're not doing a rolling fund, but this is what we're doing. And I know there were LPs who invested in our fund who read that first, right? And so now that gives them a framework of, oh, he's doing something different.

[SPEAKER_00]
Absolutely. I think the whole building in public when you're working through things, some of those things take so long to explain when you atomize the different structures on the back-end of venture and are putting them back together in a structure that works better for, you know, the modern, the next generation of fund managers, in my opinion, will choose to atomize the structures and use them like little Lego blocks and put them in all sorts of different formations. So you've talked to an incredible number of funds and GPs. I'm curious what firms you look up to as a brand that you've admired or taken a little Lego piece of.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, I'm a huge fan of the folks at Hustle Fund. I think Hustle Fund is an amazing brand. It's an amazing team. They do a really good job of supporting entrepreneurs in a very tangible way. Like I've been able to see it with some of our co-investors up front. I love those folks. I'm a big, I mean, everybody's a fan of Andreessen and folks like that, the incumbents, the Sequoias, the First Rounds. They're all a little different, but, you know, to become a top tier fund like that, that's the goal. But when I think about my fund construction, my fund construction is probably closest in line to precursor, you know. And Charles Hustle was like one of the first to really double down on this idea of pre-seed. What is pre-seed? Basically doing like 20 investments a year, you know, this larger portfolio, not as many board seats, really being supportive and helpful for their founders, you know, I love the work that, you know, Charles has done over there. And then, you know, when I start thinking about the firm I'm going to build out over time, my real, the firms I truly look up to are NEA and Greenspring Associates. And that's really particular because, you know, being based in Baltimore, many people might not know this, but two of the founders of NEA are from Baltimore. And it's originally a Maryland-based firm. And Greenspring Associates, which is a Maryland-based firm, one of the founders is the son of one of the founders of NEA. Those are the folks that I, as I was breaking into the tech ecosystem, that I heard about and got to meet first, right? Those are the folks who have been my mentors, my advisors, folks I run into at bars and get to talk deals with. Greenspring Associates recently got acquired by Stepstone, which is an amazing deal. It's like a $750 million deal kind of thing. NEA is a top-tier fund up there with the Sequoias and the Andreessons of the world. To have folks from that ilk who support me and some who are LPs in the fund, it means the world. And so I'm going to build the next large multi-stage firm based out of Baltimore. When people look at me crazy when I say that, I'm like, well, we already had two. I'm just the next generation in that line. And then as I think about, you know, I've closed my fund one and I'm looking at my fund two, my fund two is going to have a lot more elements of like a Greenspring Associates, which, you know, hopefully there'll be a lot more to come on that in the near future.

[SPEAKER_00]
That's such an incredible vision. And I have no doubt that you are the right person to carry it out. I'm wishing you all a success in that. So in terms of your investment style, why do founders choose to work with you in your own words?

[SPEAKER_01]
Founders choose to work with me because I tell them up front that they should treat me like an employee. I'm not always going to be the biggest check, but I'm going to be a meaningful one. And whatever you need help with, like, yeah, we do the VC help of, you know, I can pick up the phone and call an operator or try to find a rock star employee. But like, you got my cell phone number. Call me, text me for anything. Right? Like, yo, Mac, I need help just figuring out payroll. Okay, let's figure out payroll. Me and my co-founder had a big fight last night. Okay, let's talk about it. Hey, I got, I had this meeting with this VC. What does this mean? What do they say to me? Well, let's sit down and have a conversation. Hey, I got an angel investor who's getting on my nerves. What do I do? Well, let's talk about it. Should I do React Native or should I build a native app? Well, you know, let's have a call. Like, talk like you can use me for anything. Right? And so I think that's why entrepreneurs work with me. And then someone want to work with me just because they see the Twitter thing and they think I'm really cool. So, like, I'll take that, too.

[SPEAKER_00]
I love that. I really admired that about you and Rare Breed that you're really willing to go to work and go to bat for the founders that you support. I would love to talk about some of your recent deals. I know one just got announced, Early Bird. Do you want to talk a little bit about how you found that deal and why you're excited about it?

[SPEAKER_01]
Early Bird is an amazing one. That just got announced today, which is awesome. Alongside, you know, 776 or Alexis Ohangan and then Gemini, the Winklevoss twins, which is kind of odd. Like, those are like some names. I don't know if I'm supposed to be, you know, in the same breath of it, but I'll take it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Right? Oh, you better say that with your chest, Matt.

[SPEAKER_01]
But Early Bird's amazing because here's one of the secrets to getting into some of these really cool deals is I build relationships not just with other GPs, but with a lot of young people just breaking into venture. I was looking for somebody to talk to or talk about ideas or how you work in this industry. And so that actually came from a woman who I met who's working at another firm as a senior associate. And when she saw the deal, she brought it to me. And I thought it was amazing. I've gotten so many deals that way from, you know, the associates that people always tell you you shouldn't spend time with or you shouldn't talk to. Like, no, if you find an associate at a firm who thinks what you're building is really cool, they will be your biggest advocate. Right? And even if their firm doesn't do it, it doesn't mean they can't get you to a firm that does. Yeah. And so I was looking for.

[SPEAKER_00]
Especially when they can't push through a deal they're really passionate about to a partner meeting. I think folks find particular joy in finding a partner that believes in it as much as they do.

[SPEAKER_01]
A hundred percent. And so that's how that deal came through. And I got to meet Jordan and Caleb and amazing team, amazing founders, amazing vision. It's a cool product because, you know, it allows you to make investments on behalf of the young people in your life. The children in your life. Well, I have nine godchildren. And whenever they have a birthday or a holiday, I buy them a gift and then I buy them stock in the company that makes that gift or that gift represents. Right? Now I can do it in early bird. This just made my life easier. Right? So, like, this is already something I do. And this is something that I advocate for other people to do. Now I got a company I'm behind in support. Make that happen. Like, that's a win-win for everybody. So, I'm really bullish on them.

[SPEAKER_00]
That's awesome. Can you talk about some of the traits and founders that particularly interest you?

[SPEAKER_01]
Every deal is its own individual thing. Right? My framework is I look for exceptional people. Right? But what makes you exceptional can be different for every person. Right? Like, David Pickrell from a company called Par. They help gig workers better manage all the different platforms they use, find more work, and figure out which route is making the most money. This dude was working at a venture firm but cared about this problem so much that he was doing, like, two to four hours every day of gig work himself. And then he, like, went to another state and hung out with a gig driver who was making, like, $30 or $40 an hour routinely and just rode around with him for a week to figure out how he did it. Like, it's going, like, all these, like, off-the-beaten-path, like, chat rooms and blogs just to talk to these drivers in this community. And he's like, you care about this way too much. You are the perfect person to solve this problem. Right? And that's amazing. But then, you know, on the flip side, you got a founder like Sierra for the company Rebundle making plant-based biodegradable braiding hair because she had such a bad experience putting synthetic hair in her head. She wanted to solve a problem for it. Like, the idea of using plants to create hair that's safer on your body and better for the environment, that's just crazy. Like, who thinks like that? That's awesome. Specifically in Rebundle, the reason I made that investment, because they do have some competitors, one was they were the first ones to launch in the U.S. with the product, but two, they had a really strong brand. The founder, Sierra, spent time building her brand as an influencer in the sustainability space and then was really thoughtful about all the branding she put together for her company. It was a combination of an amazing founder with a truly amazing vision, building something unique that was hitting on some macro trends, right? Of sustainability and wanting to have better products for people of color for their hair, while also having a strong brand that was really carrying the company. And so that was, you know, all those pieces come together, that makes it an interesting one. But then, you know, we got a founder like Femi from ScholarMe, which is being rebranded soon. You know, the reason I made the investment in him is because he's the one who famously used a Venmo hack to get his first 25,000 users. He was, what, 17 when he told me he did this? Like, I knew he was smarter than me and everybody else in the room. I was just like, yeah, just give him a check and we'll see what happens. And he goes on the YC, you know, he raised money from Paul Graham personally. He just raised some significant capital. He was getting ready to raise more, you know, have a company valued at over $100 million here soon. He's a 21-year black kid from Baltimore. Like, that's incredible, right? And all I needed to know was like.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I didn't know he was from Baltimore. I got introduced to him through Vern at Real Time and Marlon at Impulse. And they were like, yo, you have to meet Femi. He's awesome. And I was just so blown away by his presence is one where you just, like, whatever he needs to do, he's going to figure it out. Like, you got it. Whatever you need to learn, you're going to learn and be so excited by it.

[SPEAKER_01]
So when I worked for the state of Maryland, I wrote him his very first check.

[SPEAKER_00]
Really?

[SPEAKER_01]
40K to drop out of college.

[SPEAKER_00]
Wow. Wow. What a crazy journey. So you've just come off a very long period of fundraising. How are you thinking of using or differently structuring your time as we're entering the wilderness part of being fund managers?

[SPEAKER_01]
Here's the thing, right? Like, I want to take a break. I want to focus on some things. I want to do some planning. But honestly, we're in a really crazy market. Things are moving really fast. Things are moving really high. And when you have momentum, you can't stop. This is actually something Charles Heson told me. You know, he's like, you know, you don't stop. If you got the momentum, you keep going. So honestly, now that fund one's closed, we're actually spending Q4 working on the strategy and putting materials for fun too. I'm excited about the potential for a larger fund where I can really bring, you know, my team on. But I'm going right back to the fundraising. And, you know.

[SPEAKER_00]
It's such a crazy story. So for context for those listening, Mac and I both participated in Joel Asset in Capital's Emerging Fund Manager Program, which is awesome. I highly recommend. And he hosted a family office summit, which is the first time I met Mac in person. And, Mac, I would love for you to share this story because I feel like it's such a great encapsulation of your dedication to venture. Sure.

[SPEAKER_01]
It's crazy. Joel asked me to moderate a panel. Like, I said, sure. And so I'm going to catch a train up to New York. But I made it so that, like, I would get to New York and I have, like, a 45-minute buffer to get to the event. So I get on the train and the train's running 10 minutes late. So we lost 10 minutes there. So 45, now 35. Cool. I get there and I call an Uber, but they want me to walk to a corner. I don't know New York. So I walk to one street. It's the wrong corner. So not only is there traffic and streets are blocked off, my driver didn't know how to get to where we need to get to. Now I'm just watching time click away, tick away, tick away. And so we get to the point where like I'm clearly late. And we're just like, standstill traffic. And so I just jumped out of the Lyft, paid the guy, and ran to where the event was being held. So I walk in in my nice dress clothes, which I hadn't worn all pandemic. And sweat pouring down, I open the door to the room. And as I open the door to the room, Joel looks at me. He's like, hey, Mac. Glad to see you here. Why don't you come up on stage and finish this? I'm just like, okay. Give me a moment to catch my breath. Let's go. So I was like 20 minutes late, but still had an amazing panel.

[SPEAKER_00]
I think it was so, so synchronous that you showed up as you got to the question where you were asking institutional LPs about the importance of investing in diverse fund managers, which was just such perfect timing. I think that was such a great way to get to finally meet each other in person. And like, as you think about building your team, I think this is like one of the things that I'm thinking about as we wrap up fund one is like, how do you scale this effort? So I'm curious, like how you're thinking about how you're selecting people to work at Rare Breed.

I'm being really lazy about it. So like to date, I have two venture partners and three fellows, all the people I either knew before I started my fund or who like chased me down and like wouldn't leave me alone until I gave them work to do. And so like at this point, it's just like, well, this team. And then there's a few associates at other firms who I've worked really closely with who have sourced deals from me. Like when I get a chance, I'm going to poach you. I'll work with the team who believed in me when, you know, other people work. So we'll see how far that gets me.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, that's really powerful. What have you learned over this past year? What have been the biggest things you've been reflecting on?

[SPEAKER_01]
One, that you can do venture differently. You don't have to follow anybody's path. Two, just do it. Like everybody, like when you want to do something that people think is crazy, you'll get a lot of naysayers. But just do it. Like just go do it. Like I didn't even know if I could raise a $10 million fund. Like if you told me I could raise a $10 million fund in less than 18 months, I told you you were crazy. But no, like I had the ability to do it because I know what I'm doing. Like this is what I do. I am a good investor. But it can be scary. Like if you're not at a big name firm and everybody already knows your name and people want to throw money at you, it's a really hard road and can be really scary. And honestly, we don't talk about this, but most people who go out to raise funds don't. Right? Most people don't hit their targets. But don't ever let anybody tell you that you can't. Right? Don't ever let anybody tell you that you're not good enough. You're self-included. I've also learned that don't let money stop you from doing things. Like if you don't have the money, just start doing it. Because if you go about it right, there will be people around to help you. Those are two tangible things I can put out there.

[SPEAKER_00]

Like, if you're an LP and you don't have the ability to write somewhere between like a $1 to $5 million check, you might miss out on some things, right? Like, you're just hoping that when I get the fund three or fund four, if I'm doing really well, that you'll get a chance to get allocation. Or you're going to have some consultant who's going to meet me at a conference who's going to then tell you that I'm great and that's how I'm going to get in front of you. Like, I get it, right? Like, the deal flows crazy on the LP side, just like it is on our side. But there needs to be more creativity around how we get money to emerging managers. And look at folks like Insight Partners or Alpaca VC or Plexo Capital, where they're doing these type of checks. And because of what happened with George Floyd, you know, Insight and Alpaca did these diversity initiatives where me and some of my peers got funding at stages where we normally wouldn't be talking to folks like that. And that's great for us emerging diverse GPs, but why don't we just have that ecosystem overall for all emerging GPs, right? I think it's a smart strategy. I think the bigger thing is don't do diversity for diversity's sake. I know several diverse individuals who got those associate roles who aren't being valued at their firm. Trust me, I get as an associate, a job can suck sometimes. It can be thankless. You're doing a lot of work. You're not investing in stuff that you always like because your job is to get stuff to the partnership, not really just because you like it. I've seen some folks have to go through hoops and do extra work and go above and beyond what their counterparts have to do because people are making the argument that they're new to venture. But you hired them because you thought they were qualified. They've been there for over a year. You haven't done a single deal of theirs. In one case, I had one of these associates. They've sourced three deals for me. I've had another one sourced two. And I know they're good deals. Follow up funding showing they're good deals. So why don't their firms appreciate the deals they're bringing up? You got to question something when things like that happen. I totally get you. Rare Breed.

[SPEAKER_00]
Rare Breed 1. What is that? You've listened to the show. You know I love kind of portfolio construction. What does that look like for you? You've got $10 million for the fund. How do you want to allocate this? How diverse in terms of, you know, concentration? How do you think about check size?

[SPEAKER_01]
So checks are $250 to $100. Really, the strategy was really doing just $250K checks because really my strategy is around doing larger checks at pre-seed. And when people ask me about ownership, I tell them it's not so much about ownership as it is about multiples. What we know is you get the highest multiples at pre-seed to seed. And then every round after that, the multiples go down. So you need to put larger dollar amounts to get higher returns. So really what we're trying to do is put in the largest check reasonable as early as possible so that we have the potential to get a large enough return to return the fund in every investment we do. Really, we're going to do somewhere between like 40 to 45 companies. You know, I'm trying to be the next lowercase. So we'll see how those returns come out.

[SPEAKER_00]
And so 40 to 45 with no reserve strategy?

[SPEAKER_01]
No, no. So we're going to do somewhere in the neighborhood of like six to 10 follow-on, but mostly most first checks. And we'll also do a few off thesis investments. You know, we got about 5% of the fund allocated for off thesis. And I'll tell you, it's funny. I have a pre-seed fund. I invest super early. Well, it just so happens that we got to be a small check in the second round of Main Street. For those who don't know, Main Street second round was a $60 million round. I got to put a $100K check on that round. Do you not know that is the deal that gets most LPs excited? It's not even my strategy. It's just the fact that for me, it's all about quality of deal. And so if it's a quality deal, I need to take a look at it. And Main Street was amazing. You know, the strategy is some off thesis things for like really opportunistic quality investments, but mostly it's companies outside major tech hubs, outside of Silicon Valley, New York and Massachusetts, North America, South America, and the UK for these founders that are just typically overlooked. And sometimes founders that aren't overlooked, but just building great companies. People ask me sometimes, what makes Rare Breed different and unique? That's like, we invest in everybody. Like the idea that I could say that's even incredible as a differentiator, but like I invest in everybody. It doesn't matter. One of my top performing companies right now is a company based out of Memphis, Tennessee called BeautyByMe.io with a founder who changes his nail color three times a day and go plays basketball after work every day. And he's incredible. Charles is incredible. The company he's building is going to truly revolutionize the beauty industry in ways that I don't even think he understands. He's just in Memphis, Tennessee trying to figure it out.

[SPEAKER_00]
You know, when you had Rare Breed in your mind and you were thinking about what it would be like, what's the biggest challenges and what've been the biggest surprises?

[SPEAKER_01]
The biggest challenge was getting over my feelings of being inadequate. I don't have a college degree. I don't have a finance background. You know, I got into this in a really unconventional way. For a long time, I was concerned about whether or not I could do this or if people were going to respect me or if people were going to care about my firm and I could get follow-on funding from my companies. That was just me inside my own head. The other thing that was a challenge was like finding LPs. Like I didn't have a network of LPs. So like, thank you, Twitter. And thank you, 506C. Like if not for 506C and my ability to publicly solicit, like I don't know if this happens. And I think the last thing was, I mentioned being a broke VC. I figured that if you gave me 24 months and I could talk to enough people, I could figure out a way to raise 10 million. Like give me enough time, I figured it out. But one of the issues that held me back early on was I didn't have the money to do the traveling to raise a fund. COVID being what it was and everybody being stuck in the house actually helped me. I had all my meetings over Zoom. I didn't have any in-person meetings, so I didn't have to travel. So I got to save that money. If it wasn't for that, I actually wouldn't have had the money just to go to like meetings in New York every other week or fly across the country to go meet with like, I didn't have

[SPEAKER_00]
that. And so I got lucky. Can I ask on the feelings of inadequacy side, I've had a team. But my question to you is what helped you get over that? Was it the Twitter accreditation? Was it the support from GPs? What allowed you to break that barrier?

[SPEAKER_01]
It was a little bit of all that. You know, the Twitter thing was very reassuring. Meeting with other GPs and, you know, talking, shopping, realizing like I can go toe to toe with everybody here. But I also think in August 2019, I went through 500 Startups VC Unlocked program based at Stanford. And it's basically, you know, for two weeks, you and a bunch of peers are learning from these Stanford professors about venture. While I was there, I recognized very early on, like I knew most of this stuff. I could do all of this. I'm having conversations with these professors far beyond what we're doing in the class. And one of the professors, Trevor, pulled me to the side one day. He's like, man, you can do this. He's like, you're as good. You can do this as well as I can. You know all this material. If you want to raise a fund, I don't understand why you haven't already. That validation in those moments was so impactful. Having somebody who I look up to and respect and it's already been in venture for years, being like, yeah, you can do this. And being in these classrooms and like, oh yeah, I understand all these concepts. It reminded me of the time I actually went back to school. Like there was a time I went back to school and I went to Strayer University, you know, online college. And I took a database administration course. And I was like, everybody in the class is like, I'm taking this class because one day I want to be a DBA. And they got to me like, I'm a DBA trying to finish school. And I'm just sitting in the class like, I could have taught this class. Yeah, I'm not doing this college thing again. It was just like the same kind of moment again. And so that was really helpful. Yeah. That's how I got over it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Can I ask you one? And again, imposter syndrome to being more successful as you are now. Do you ever worry that kind of, you can kind of believe the hype and actually this grit that you have in the early days and that I'm going to make this work and it's just hell fire, whatever it is, nothing's going to stop me. You can almost become a little bit lethargic with success.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. But I think I've had enough failures in my life to know I need to stay grounded. Even now, my portfolio is doing well. We've gotten several early markups and everybody's like, oh, this is amazing. This fund's going to be great. And I'm like, eh, until we get returns, none of this matters. This all looks good on paper, but what matters is returns. And so it could look good today. It could look good for the next three years and it could all bottom out after that. And keeping that perspective and always reminding my team and the folks helping me helps me stay level because it is easy to get caught up in the hype. When I was working for the investment arm for the state of Maryland, we started this pre-seed fund for underrepresented founders and it got all this hype and everybody's excited. Like, oh, you're doing these amazing things. The first three companies we invested in went straight to zero. Like my first three, straight to zero. The next six, all still alive today. Three of them are in my current portfolio. But that was a humbling experience. Like, oh, we can do this. We know what we're doing. We're going to chase the game. We're going to do this amazing thing. First three, zeros, right off the bat. You can't start off any worse than that. You can only go up from there.

[SPEAKER_00]
But I do want to ask you, I said about the challenge that, what about the biggest surprise?

[SPEAKER_01]
The biggest surprise has been Twitter. I've been on Twitter since 2010. Last June, I had 2,500 followers, right? Like 10 years, 2,500 people. I went from 2,500, I think I just crossed 50,000 like yesterday. And it's been surreal. Having done the Twitter thing and interacted with so many folks over a short amount of time, I would have folks I'd be meeting with telling me how all these people in their firm are talking about me. I'm like, but you work at like a top tier firm. How do they even know who I am? Why do people care what I have to say? I've gotten on calls and like, I've had people like burst into tears because they're meeting me. You probably have, you probably had some of this before. It's like, I'm just another emerging manager trying to do good work. Like, I ain't special. I ain't a celebrity. Nothing like that. That's been kind of, and then, you know, because of that, I've now gotten to have a podcast with inside. I've had like four or five different people reach out to me about doing TV shows. It's just like, just because I got people to listen to me on Twitter, like my whole life is changing. That was like a crazy surprise.

[SPEAKER_00]
I do want to ask that, you know, we spoke about Rare Breed and the structure and the strategy. A lot of people are talking about rolling funds. How do you feel about the rise of rolling funds? And why did you decide not to do a rolling fund?

[SPEAKER_01]
I think rolling funds are another sign of the lack of innovation in our industry. Like, Angel's List took something that had been around before that people weren't really using. They took a designation of 506C, which had been around since 2013, that nobody was really using and kind of pushed it together and made a product to help emerging manager or give another structure for fundraising. And it's like, everybody's like, oh my God, this is so world changing. It's like, well, should we be doing stuff like this from the regular? Should we be digging about how to come up with stuff like this often? If this is the biggest innovation we can point to, that's sad, right? But then the other thing for me was I looked at rolling funds. I thought they were really interesting. They would allow me to take advantage of like growing Twitter following and such. But what I didn't like about rolling funds was the way they do LP returns. Like LPs have to continuously buy in the quarters to make sure they get allocation to the companies you invest in. So if you're not an LP in the specific quarter, and that's the quarter I make my best investment in, but you're an LP in the quarter before or the quarter after, you don't get access to that deal or to those returns. And I knew for me that a lot of my earliest LPs were just going to be people who truly supported me and cared about me. And some of them were going to be writing small checks. So if you write me a small 10K check and you can only spread that across four quarters, then that means if I make a really good investment in quarter five or beyond, you don't get access to that. But in a traditional fund, you get access to every deal I do over the life of that fund. I needed to make sure I was going to be equitable to all my LPs. And I couldn't put them on the wheel of like, well, you gave me 10K for these first four quarters. If you want to get into the next deal, you got to put up another 10K. Like I didn't want to do that to folks. But I did still want all the advantages. And so I created a fund, this traditional fund. We used 506C so I could publicly solicit. We worked with Carter as our backend. Carter told us they were partnering with a company called Anduin Transactions, which turns your sub docs into a guided web form. And so we made a website that had a button that says, click here to become an LP. And if you do and tell me you're accredited, you get access to my sub docs. It's that easy. Go to our websites, click a button. You get to our sub docs. You can sign up to be an LP. I've had quite a few LPs signed up to be LPs without ever talking to me. And so I have to like double back and talk to them after the fact. And then I told Carter, I was like, look, I want access to capital. Kind of like how rolling funds do. They give you that first quarter as you go. I was like, I'm going to do a rolling close every three weeks. So as our LPs come in, I just want you to close on them. I actually wanted to do it every week. And they were like, can you give us a better cadence like every three weeks? I was like, sure, we can do that. Additional fund that gave me all the advantages of a rolling fund without any of the disadvantages. Because all the disadvantages were structural. All the advantages were all like technological. So it's just running with it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, we spoke about the kind of structural lessons there, how you did that. Love that, actually. And I'm totally with you. I think the biggest mistake people make is they don't take LP cash off the table and they leave it for too long. And then people forget about it and say, ah, I actually allocated it elsewhere. And, you know, you lose some then. You know, you've had a lot from the challenges to the surprises to the lessons on the structure. When you think about advising managers today, what do you know now that you wish you'd known when you were at Maryland? When you were starting Rare Breed in the first day? What's the, oh, I wish I had known this when I started?

[SPEAKER_01]
Fundraising is going to be one of the hardest things you ever have to do. Everybody's going to tell you that and it's going to be harder than that. So just know that going in. Understand that all the strategies and advice you're getting, it's all great. But you don't have to follow any of it. You don't have to do any of it. You can create your own structures. Like the same way I decided I was going to change the way I was going to do my fundraising and my structure. You can do the same thing. You don't have to follow these traditional rules that everybody says we have to do. You can be innovative. You can be innovative with your fund. You can be innovative with your structure. I mean, you can look at somebody like Will Zell from Zell Capital. He created an access fund. He worked with the SEC to create a fund where you could publicly solicit and you could take as many LPs as you want. Like from anybody, including retail investors. I mean, that's innovative. Like what Will's doing some crazy stuff. You can put in the work to kind of structure or fund the way you want it to be. You don't have to follow all these antiquated notions and advice that you get. So be bold. Be very bold.

[SPEAKER_00]
Be very bold. What do you want to build with Ravreed? Like if we do this show in 10 years time, what is Ravreed?

[SPEAKER_01]
So I love this question because I'm going to build the next NEA, the next Spring, Spring Associates, the next top tier firm. And I use those two firms very specifically because what I don't think many people recognize is both of those are Baltimore-based firms. Two of the three founders of NEA are from Baltimore. They used to have originally NEA as a Maryland-based firm. One of the founders of Greenspring is the sign of one of the founders of NEA. And those are people who are my mentors, my advisors, the folks who will help me in my career. And so I am built on the shoulder of giants. You're going to look up 10 years from now and we're going to be building the next top tier multi-stage firm based out of Baltimore. And that's what it's going to be.

[SPEAKER_00]
Final one before the quick find. It's like every firm says, what is it? You know, entrepreneurship is unevenly distributed and amazing people come from anywhere and all of this. Do you find that's the case when you look at follow-on funding and you give it to your top tier series A's, B's, C's? Do you find that actually they are fully embracing Maryland, Texas? You name your, I don't know America very well. It's okay. Middle America.

[SPEAKER_01]
Or are they like, ah, it's not in New York or not for us. They care about money. So if you have strong enough metrics, they find a way to get over themselves no matter where you're from. And that's why I tell my founders, like, hey, there may be biases against you. People may say, if you don't live close enough to us or if you're not in New York or Silicon Valley, you can't find top tier talent. But if you're growing by 40% month over month and you got strong margins and the business looks like it's unstoppable, you'll get a check from somebody somewhere. So if you focus on that, everything will be all right. And that way, I don't have to think about the series A folks are doing. As long as I help my companies be as strong and grow as fast as they can, it'll happen.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I'd take 40% month on month. That worked for me. Thanks, Mac. Absolutely. I do want to move into my favorite, as you know, the quickfire. So I'm going to say a short statement. You hit me with your thoughts. Sound good? Sounds good. Okay. So you've listened to the show before. What's the favorite book and why?

[SPEAKER_01]
Favorite book and why? Why should white guys have all the fun? Because Reginald F. Lewis being a black man from Baltimore who created a private equity firm and was a billionaire is somebody who I look up to and respect. And just earlier this week, I got to speak at the Harvard Club where he was a member. And it was like a full circle moment to be in the same hallways that he walked and where he celebrated his wins. And even more cooler than that was afterwards, I tweeted about it and his daughter posted about it on Instagram, which is like kind of surreal for me. So why should white guys have all the fun? Because Reginald F. Lewis was a pioneer.

[SPEAKER_00]
Tell me, when shit hits the fan, how do you deal with it?

[SPEAKER_01]
When shit hits the fan, I call up my friends, tell them we should go to Buffalo Wild Wings and go have a drink and have a beer or two and some spicy hot wings. Talk to my friends, vent about it, go back and answer some emails. I think it's a lot cheaper than my therapist.

[SPEAKER_00]
Tell me, what's the hardest element of your role with Rare Breed today?

[SPEAKER_01]
The hardest element of my role at Rare Breed today is figuring out how to be present for my family. This job is so all-consuming. And once you decide you're going to start a firm, you're basically making a 20-year commitment, right? Fund one's 10 years. Two, three years later, you're going to raise fund two. That's another 10 years. Two to three years after that, you're going to raise fund three. You're now 17 years in that you're dedicated. And it's a hard job. It takes a lot of time and a lot of effort. And so it makes it hard to be present at home when you have a family, you have a significant other, when you have children. Trying to make sure I give them the highest quality of time because I know I can't give them the quantity of time. That's been a struggle.

[SPEAKER_00]
What would you most like to change about the world of venture? There's many things, I'm sure, but what would you most?

[SPEAKER_01]
I want venture to be more diverse on the LP side, the GP side, all the way through. And I would love for venture to give founders, especially first-time founders and diverse founders, more grace for not knowing every little thing about this industry. Like if a founder gives you an NDA, don't go crazy on them. Don't end the meeting. Use it as a teachable moment to explain to them like, why we don't do that? So many VCs don't take just the simplest five minutes to explain why they don't sign NDA. Things like that. I wish we would be more thoughtful about being people.

[SPEAKER_00]
Penultimate one, you can have a billboard anywhere in the world and it can say anything on it. What do you want on that billboard and where is it?

[SPEAKER_01]
It's probably in New York City somewhere because that's where most people are going to see it. And it's going to say, wear a mask, get vaccinated. Let's all do this together because I miss going to bars and clubs and happy hours and everything else I love to do with my friends and family. So let's all work together so we can get back to a normal. I'm tired of saying new normal. I just want to go back to normal.

[SPEAKER_00]
But I do one final one and it's as you know, what's the most recent publicly announced investment? And why did you say yes and get so excited?

[SPEAKER_01]
Most recently publicly announced investment was an investment in a company called Unspun out of Oakland. If you go to their website, it shows that they make custom jeans. They have an app that scans your body, your jeans that made to fit. And what they're actually building is in the background is they have a hardware component that takes the information from the app of your sizing and basically 3D prints your clothes. And one piece was zero waste. When I first met the founders, they were just incredible people who were truly passionate about this. And they were building a tool that could revolutionize manufacturing all across the globe. And then they had a letter of support from like the head of design from Levi saying, my job is to figure out how to make the best jeans and they do better than me. They're like, I'm okay, I'm in. Like, that works for me, right? This is a combination of the amazing people, the ambitious goal, and then the support they have behind them. And I should also say that company was sourced by my venture partner, Jonathan Kroll. Shout out Jonathan. You know, he was truly bullish on this company and wanted to get it done. And so we were going to do it regardless because, you know, if somebody on my team truly believes that strongly, then I believe in conviction. Like, if you have that strong enough conviction, I'll ride with you every time. But he was right. He was so right. They're such a great team.

[SPEAKER_00]
Listen, Max, as I said, I'm so pleased that we connected over Twitter. I'm so pleased that we got to do this show. So thank you so much for joining me today. And this has been a lot of fun.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank you for having me, Harry. I really appreciate it. Again, like, I can't believe I'm here. I'm on the show. Like, mama, I made it. I'm on 20 Minute VC.

[SPEAKER_00]
Such a fun episode to do there with Mac and can't wait to see all that he builds with Rarebreed. If you'd like to see more from us behind the scenes, of course you can on the 20minutevc.com. I always love to see you there. But before we leave you today, Mercury is building full stack banking for startups, applying under 10 minutes from anywhere for FDIC-insured bank accounts, physical and virtual debit cards, domestic and international wires, and integrations with Gusto, Stripe, QuickBooks, Plaid, basically every other tool your startup uses. They also offer unusual features like API access, custom team management, and their newly launched Mercury Treasury, a cash management product for high-growth startups. They'll even help you build your startup with Mercury Raise, a program to connect you to Silicon Valley's top investors. Head over to mercury.com forward slash sign up to apply today. And speaking of crucial infrastructure for your business with Mercury, do you want to spend less time vying for tech talent and more time building world-class products? Well, that's where my friends at Terminal come in. Terminal helps fast-growing tech companies rapidly scale engineering teams so you can focus on innovating. They do this by providing you with a pipeline, pre-vetted global remote talent, currently 90,000 and growing, and a remote management platform that handles all localized admin, legal and HR support, so you don't take on the legal risks and operational headaches. To date, Terminal has hired hundreds of developers based in Canada and Latin America that are fully remote, full-time employees at high-growth companies like Gusto, Chime, Earning, and Hims. To learn more about how you can scale your engineering talent today, go to terminal.io. And last but by no means least, I have to say I just love using AngelList's fund admin platform to manage my investments. The team and the platform at AngelList takes care of all my back-office needs so that I can focus on working with great founders. Leading fund managers have made over 10,000 investments into 6,000 startups via AngelList, all online and all in one place. And with the recently announced rolling funds, you can easily find and invest in these top managers on AngelList.com forward slash rolling. As always, I so appreciate all your support and I can't wait to bring you the first ever completely unscripted, unscheduled episode on Thursday. It's a very special one with Ryan Dennehy at electric.ai.

A lot of people have missed a lot of bets. Even some of the bets that they've taken haven't necessarily panned out. And I would argue that the reason for that has a lot to do with just human nature. Yeah, I think in a lot of ways, the landscape is being reimagined. And there's an abundance. I'm a former consultant. Yeah, well, obviously, I think this, this goes back to, like, just Adam. Like, the third point I would have made about him was the same as you're making. It's like, even if you don't think he'd differ on people, you, you can't say with a straight face that he is, like, morally incorruptible. Like, he did make some morally questionable decisions. And he seems to have a habit of hedging his bets and, like, self-dealing and doing whatever it takes to provide the best returns for Adam and not for his company. And although, historically, you know, many of the venture capitalists who've worked with him have still done well, that's not generally the recipe for success. Like, normally, you want to be all in on the company you're building and, you know, have some sort of undivided loyalty to that company. And Adam just hasn't shown that. With WeWork, even in the early days, like, the stories of him, you know, raising his own salary or buying assets from himself or, like, there's a lot of weird stories that went around. And I don't know how many of them are true, but there was a lot that made it seem as if he was always putting himself above the company. And definitely, the way he treated employees or the way that he, you know, went about making certain acquisitions made it seem as if he was making them for his personal use more than the business use. So, I'm not going to, I'm not going to, like, comment specifically on what he is doing because I definitely don't have enough information to go out and, you know, criticize what he is doing currently. But I will say that you have a person with a history of self-dealing and of doing what is in his interest over the interest of investors in the company. And it seems like that person is continuing to do that and is backing multiple horses in an industry that he thinks will succeed. I don't know if that's the case, but that's what it seems like. And if it is, it seems to me that he hasn't really learned his lesson. And at the end of the day, if you look at this from an outside party's perspective, he's going to win. One of the two companies wins. Like, there's multiple companies with hundreds of millions of dollars and one of them will probably win. Like, he's going to walk away with a lot of money. Will Andreessen Horowitz and his other venture capital, you know, backers walk away with anything? That's, like, the question. And then, you know, it takes us back to why they would make that investment in the first place because it's the way he's going to act. So, yeah, I think it's a complicated scenario, but I think it's a bit too early to pass judgment and we don't have enough information to, like, fully understand what's going on. But if that is the case and he's kind of put himself in a position where he's going to win and maybe his investors will or won't, that's definitely not something that, as a VC, if I saw that, I would have any interest in working with someone like that.

[SPEAKER_00]
Adam, you're not a great person. I just want you to know that. Would I back you? Probably not. Are you going to make a lot of money? You probably will. That's the part that sucks. And that money could be very well better used for founders and funders that look like me and Liam, but, hey, it is what it is, folks. But with that, I hope you've enjoyed another amazing edition of Building Out Loud podcast. I am your host, Matt, the VC, with my partner, lawyer, Liam, a.k.a. Liam Gill. Liam, before we roll out,

[SPEAKER_01]
you got any last notes for the folks? I think we covered it pretty in-depthly. I'm going to be pretty interested to see how this all plays out. I really like, the question I have right now is if Flo is pitched as a tech company, which is actually a real estate company and he's redoing the whole WeWork scam in a housing market, or if he's actually pitched as a real estate company and Andreessen's happy with a 3 or 4x and that's what's happening. It's really, it would be insanely cool to know how that went and what was promised to those investors because you would think that if they think they're going to get the type of WeWork returns that were promised sort of when the Vision Fund came in that investors would know better. But as you said, even if they weren't promised that, even if they were promised less, given the amount of money Andreessen has to invest, if they thought they were going to get 4x on it, it's definitely a good investment for them.

[SPEAKER_00]
That's what it is. Well, we'll see you next time. Make sure you subscribe and review. Let's, you know, trick these algorithms. So, subscribe, unsubscribe, resubscribe, resubscribe, unsubscribe, all that good stuff. Show everybody how amazing we are. Make sure you tell your friends. If you leave us a five-star review with a comment, we may just read it on the podcast. Get yourself in here. You know, we might start doing a mailbag, but the mailbag will be from comments left with five-star reviews. So, make sure you let everybody know how great we are. If you want to email us, hit us up at buildingoutloudpodcast at gmail.com. Don't worry, Liam reads them all and gets to them, you know, so you got to worry about me and my crazy busy inbox schedule and all the good stuff. Make sure you hit us up on Twitter, MacDVC, Lawyer Liam, and we'll see you next time, folks. Peace out, y'all.

[None]
Peace out, y'all.
